**By James Masters, CNN**
**HYLANDS PARK, England (CNN) —** Exactly 100 years after a British war hero took 20 boys to a wind-swept island to teach them tracking and camping, a sea of neckerchiefs from over 150 nations has transformed the English countryside into a temporary city of youth. 

More than 40,000 young people gathered at Hylands Park in Essex on Wednesday for the 21st World Scout Jamboree, marking the official centenary of the global Scouting movement. At precisely 8:00 a.m. local time, millions of Scouts around the world simultaneously renewed their Scout Promise in a synchronized "Scouting Sunrise" ceremony.

"When Robert Baden-Powell started that first experimental camp in 1907, he couldn’t have envisioned this," said World Scout Committee Chairman Philippe Da Costa, looking out over a tent city spanning 700 acres. "What began as an experiment has become the largest youth movement in human history."

### From Small Island to Global Stage

The movement’s origins trace back to August 1, 1907, when Baden-Powell, a lieutenant general in the British Army, brought a group of boys from diverse background to Brownsea Island off the southern coast of England. Drawing on his military experiences and outdoorsmanship, he published *Scouting for Boys* in 1908—a book that unexpectedly became an instant bestseller and sparked an international phenomenon.

A century later, the Organization of the Scout Movement boasts more than 28 million members across 160 countries, with only a handful of nations—such as North Korea and Cuba—prohibiting the organization. 

For the Scouts assembled in Essex, the movement is less about history and more about shared connection.

"I’m sharing a tent with a guy from Japan and another from Brazil," said 16-year-old Marcus Vance, a Boy Scout from Chicago. "We speak different languages at home, but here, we all know the same knots, the same songs, and the same values. It’s pretty mind-blowing."

### Adapting to a Changing World

While the image of Scouting has long been tied to campfires, compasses, and wooden neckerchief slides, modern leaders stress that the movement has evolved to meet 21st-century challenges.

Today’s Scouts earn badges not just in knot-tying and fire-starting, but in information technology, environmental science, and global development. In recent years, Scouting organizations worldwide have placed a heavy emphasis on community service, aiding in flood relief efforts in Asia, tree-planting initiatives in Africa, and urban renewal projects in North America.

"Scouting is not just about surviving in the wilderness anymore," said Dr. Eduardo Missoni, Secretary General of the World Organization of the Scout Movement (WOSM). "It is about creating active global citizens. We are teaching young people how to navigate a complex, interconnected world."

### Facing Modern Challenges

Despite its massive global footprint, the movement enters its second century facing modern headwinds. In several Western nations, including the United States and the United Kingdom, Scouting has struggled with declining youth enrollment in an era dominated by digital screens and structured youth sports. 

The movement has also faced intense public debates in some countries regarding inclusivity, modernizing traditional gender roles, and secularization. 

However, growth in developing regions—particularly in Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa—has propelled global membership to record highs. Countries like Indonesia now host the world's largest Scout populations.

### 'Be Prepared' for the Next 100 Years

As the sun set over the Jamboree encampment on Wednesday evening, lighting up thousands of fires and portable cooking stoves, the atmosphere remained triumphantly forward-looking. 

A video message from former Scouts—including astronauts, world leaders, and celebrities—was broadcast across giant screens to the crowd of teenagers, urging them to carry Baden-Powell’s famous motto, "Be Prepared," into a new century.

For 15-year-old Amara Okafor, a Girl Guide from Lagos, Nigeria, the message of the centenary was simple.

"The world has a lot of problems right now," Okafor said, adjusting her green neckerchief. "But if you look around this park, you realize that millions of us are being trained to help fix them. That gives me hope for the next hundred years."

It was here, on August 1, 1907, that a decorated British army officer named Lieutenant-General Robert Baden-Powell brought 20 boys from diverse social backgrounds for an experimental eight-day camping trip. He wanted to test ideas he had written about in a military handbook, adapting them to teach young people outdoor skills, teamwork, and self-reliance.

On Wednesday morning, two Scouts selected from every country in the world gathered on the exact field where Baden-Powell pitched his first tents. The story of Scouting is inextricably linked to Baden-Powell, known affectionately to generations of Scouts as "B-P." 

A hero of the Boer War following his successful defense of the town of Mafeking, Baden-Powell returned to Britain to find that a small manual he had written for soldiers, *Aids to Scouting*, was surprisingly popular among young boys and teachers.

What Baden-Powell envisioned as a weekend activity for British boys quickly crossed borders and genders. By 1910, his sister Agnes—and later his wife Olave—helped form the Girl Guides (known in the U.S. as Girl Scouts) to accommodate the thousands of young women demanding to join the movement.

"He didn't lecture them; he gave them practical skills, placed them in leadership roles, and told them to 'leave the world a little better than you found it.' That message is just as powerful today as it was in 1907."

While the centenary honors a century of tradition, leaders of the movement emphasize that Scouting must continue to adapt to the 21st century. Modern Scouts focus heavily on human rights, technology, disaster relief, and climate change, alongside traditional skills like knot-tying and wilderness survival.

"Scouting isn't just a history lesson," said 17-year-old Sarah Al-Mansoor from Kuwait. "It’s about what we do tomorrow. The world has a lot of problems, but tonight, seeing 40,000 of us united, I think the future looks pretty bright."

### **The UK: Hallowed Ground and Global Jamborees**

As the birthplace of the movement, the United Kingdom served as the epicenter of the global celebrations. The focal point was Hylands Park in Essex, which transformed into a temporary city of 40,000 young people from over 150 nations for the 21st World Scout Jamboree. 

On August 1—designated as the "Scouting Sunrise"—every Scout at the Jamboree, along with millions worldwide, renewed their Scout Promise. On Brownsea Island, two Scouts from every country in the world gathered for a solemn rededication ceremony. 

Prince William and the Duke of Kent attended the events, but the true stars were the youth. The UK celebrations blended traditional woodcraft with modern technology, featuring solar-powered campsites, global radio broadcasts, and discussions on climate change. 

"Scouting began on a tiny island with a handful of boys," declared then-UK Chief Scout Peter Duncan to a roaring crowd in Essex. "Today, it belongs to the world."

---

### **Romania: A Symbol of Freedom and Rebirth**

For *Cercetașii României* (the National Organization of Romanian Scouts), the 2007 centenary carried a profound political and emotional weight. Scouting had been banned in Romania during the communist era, suppressed for decades before being triumphantly revived in 1990 following the fall of Nicolae Ceaușescu. 

To mark the 100th anniversary, Romanian Scouts turned the celebration into a festival of youth empowerment and democratic identity. In Bucharest, central parks were taken over by interactive "Scout Villages," where youth demonstrated pioneering skills, emergency response, and community work to the public. 

High in the Carpathian Mountains, hundreds of Scouts braved rugged terrains to perform Sunrise Ceremonies at peak altitudes. As the sun rose over the Bucegi crests, young Romanians placed custom centennial markers along hiking trails. For Romania, the centenary was not just a celebration of Baden-Powell’s vision, but a celebration of the country's own regained freedoms and its re-integration into the global community.

---

### **Namibia: Service in the Arid Wilderness**

In Southern Africa, the *Scouts of Namibia* celebrated the centenary by aligning Baden-Powell’s ethos with the immediate social needs of their developing nation. Against the dramatic backdrop of the Namib Desert and the outskirts of Windhoek, Namibian Scouts marked the 100th year through action rather than mere pageantry.

In the lead-up to August 1, Scouts across Namibia embarked on massive community service initiatives. Recognizing the modern challenges facing African youth, the Namibian Scout Association integrated peer-to-peer HIV/AIDS education and reproductive health workshops into their centennial camps. 

On the morning of the Sunrise Ceremony, Scouts gathered in places ranging from urban Windhoek to remote, dusty villages in the Ovamboland region. Dressed in their distinctive beige uniforms and colorful neckerchiefs, they raised the national flag alongside the World Scout flag. 

"In Namibia, Scouting is a lifeline," reflected a local troop leader during a centennial rally in Swakopmund. "Celebrating 100 years means showing how Scouting keeps young people safe, healthy, and focused on serving their communities."

---

### **India: Massive Scale and Multi-Faith Harmony**

Few places demonstrated the staggering scale of modern Scouting like India. *The Bharat Scouts and Guides*, one of the largest national scouting organizations in the world, brought millions of youth together in a display of cultural diversity and civic duty.

Centenary celebrations kicked off with a massive National Jamboree, but the enthusiasm trickled down to every state, from the snow-capped Himalayas of Himachal Pradesh to the coastal villages of Kerala. In New Delhi, thousands of Scouts assembled at the national headquarters for a grand rally featuring traditional dances, drill displays, and a massive renewal of the Promise in multiple languages.

Environmental stewardship was the cornerstone of India’s centenary response. Scouts across the subcontinent marked the 100th anniversary by planting over a million trees in a single day—a project aimed at combating deforestation and urban heat. 

Crucially, in a country rich in religious diversity, Indian Scouts used the centenary to promote interfaith harmony. Sunrise Ceremonies in India featured readings from Hindu, Muslim, Sikh, Christian, and Buddhist scriptures, embodying the Scout Law's commitment to respecting all faiths.

---

### **A Century of Looking Forward**

When Robert Baden-Powell wrote *Scouting for Boys* in 1908, he envisioned a program to build character in British youth. He could not have predicted that a century later, young people in post-communist Eastern Europe, arid Southern Africa, dense Indian metropolises, and the English countryside would all stand at the same hour, raise three fingers, and promise to "leave the world a little better than they found it."

The 2007 centenary proved that Scouting was far from a relic of the Edwardian era. Instead, as the sun crossed the globe on August 1, it illuminated a movement that had successfully reinvented itself as a force for global citizenship, environmental action, and peace.

**CNN.com** | International Edition

# One Movement, One Promise: 28 Million Scouts Synchronize Clocks for Centenary ‘Sunrise’

**By Sarah Jenkins, CNN**
**UPDATED:** 11:42 AM EDT, Wednesday, August 1, 2007

**HYLANDS PARK, England (CNN)** — As dawn broke over the fog-shrouded coast of southern England on Wednesday, a single trumpet blew, signaling the start of an unprecedented global milestone. 

At precisely 8:00 a.m. local time, millions of youth across the globe raised three fingers in a traditional salute. From the windswept shores of Dorset to the urban parks of Tokyo, the peak of Mount Kilimanjaro, and the beaches of Rio de Janeiro, an estimated 28 million Scouts simultaneously renewed their Scout Promise, marking exactly 100 years since the birth of the world’s largest youth movement.

The global event, dubbed "Scouting’s Sunrise," kicked off a day of international celebration centered around the 21st World Scout Jamboree in Essex, England, where over 38,000 teenagers from 158 countries are currently camped. 

However, the emotional heart of the centenary remained 100 miles south on Brownsea Island—the tiny, 500-acre patch of land in Poole Harbour where British military hero Lord Robert Baden-Powell held his experimental 9-day camp for 20 boys in August 1907.

"Standing right here on the same patch of grass where it all started a hundred years ago gives me chills," said Sarah Lin, a 15-year-old Scout from London who was selected to represent the UK at the historic Brownsea Island ceremony. "Baden-Powell couldn't have imagined that 20 boys in wool caps would turn into tens of millions of us today. We are literally connected to kids in every corner of the planet right now."

### A Handbook That Changed the World

The spark that ignited this global phenomenon was a 1908 book titled *Scouting for Boys*, written by Baden-Powell following the success of his experimental island camp. Originally published in six fortnightly installments, the manual was intended to adapt military reconnaissance skills into games for youth self-reliance, wilderness survival, and citizenship.

Few literary works in history have had such an immediate, worldwide impact. *Scouting for Boys* rapidly became a runaway bestseller, ultimately claiming a spot as the fourth best-selling book of the 20th century, surpassed only by the Bible, the Koran, and the works of Shakespeare. Translated into dozens of languages, the book transformed what Baden-Powell envisioned as an auxiliary training program for existing youth groups into a self-starting, worldwide grassroots movement.

"I read a modern translation of *Scouting for Boys* back home," said Mateo Alvarez, a 16-year-old Scout from Argentina, speaking from the bustling encampment at Hylands Park. "Some of the 1908 language is funny, but the core idea—that young people can make the world better by taking care of nature and each other—is totally relevant today. It’s not just about tying knots; it’s about peace."

### From Edwardian Roots to a Modern Global Network

While Scouting began as an Edwardian-era organization primarily for British boys, the movement today looks vastly different. Co-educational in most nations, Scouting currently operates in all but four of the world's independent countries (Andorra, Cuba, Laos, and North Korea). 

At the World Jamboree in Essex, the sheer diversity of the movement was on full display following the promise renewal. Teenagers in traditional neckerchiefs exchanged badges, sang songs in dozens of languages, and discussed modern global issues, including climate change and community poverty relief.

"People think Scouts are just about camping and selling cookies," Alvarez added, adjusting his flag-draped neckerchief. "But today, 28 million of us promised to build a better world. If you put that many young people together with a single promise, you can actually change the future."

As the sun continues its path west today, the wave of promise renewals will conclude on the remote islands of the Pacific, closing out the first century of Scouting—and, as organizers insist, launching the next.
